notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 107:1–22, drawn from the sources I was able to access. Where limits prevented me from reaching certain traditions, I have noted this at the end.

---

## Overview of the Psalm

Most commentators agree that Psalm 107 is a liturgy of thanksgiving built around four vivid pictures of human distress and divine deliverance: wanderers in the desert (vv. 4–9), prisoners in chains (vv. 10–16), the sick near death (vv. 17–22), and sailors in a storm (vv. 23–32, beyond our scope). Each scene follows the same pattern: trouble → cry to the Lord → deliverance → call to give thanks. Spurgeon calls it “a choice song for the redeemed of the Lord” and notes that though it celebrates providential deliverances, “under cover of this, it mainly magnifies the Lord for spiritual blessings, of which temporal favours are but types and shadows.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

Ellicott notes that the psalm likely had the return from Babylonian exile primarily in mind (see vv. 2–3), but that the pictures are not strictly historical — they are “a lyric embodiment of the lessons of the Captivity” applied to “the human lot generally.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/107.htm

The four-fold cry-and-deliverance pattern (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28) is viewed by Constable as an answer to Solomon’s temple-dedication prayer (1 Kings 8:46–53) and a foreshadowing of Jesus’ earthly ministry, which produces the same kinds of deliverance.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-107.html

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.”

This verse is a liturgical doxology that also opens Psalms 106, 118 and 136. Spurgeon says: “It is all we can give him, and the least we can give; therefore let us diligently render to him our thanksgiving.” He explains that the Hebrew name JEHOVAH is used, and God is not to be worshipped “with groans and cries, but with thanks, for he is good … by nature, and essence, and proven to be good in all the acts of his eternity.” On “His mercy endureth for ever,” Spurgeon notes that the supplied word “endureth” somewhat restricts the sense: “better seen if we read it, ‘for his mercy for ever.’ That mercy had no beginning, and shall never know an end.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that the phrase “His mercy endures forever” is used over 30 times in the Psalms and has “almost a liturgical quality,” praising God’s covenant love (Hebrew *chesed*).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### vv. 2–3 — “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the lands…”

**v. 2:** Spurgeon writes: “Whatever others may think or say, the redeemed have overwhelming reasons for declaring the goodness of the Lord. Theirs is a peculiar redemption, and for it they ought to render peculiar praise.” He emphasises the divine agency: “His own unaided arm has wrought out their deliverance. Should not emancipated slaves be grateful to the hand which set them free?” Guzik notes the phrase “redeemed from the hand of the enemy” likely connects with the exile of God’s people, and cites Romaine (via Spurgeon) on the Hebrew *goel* — the near-kinsman who had the right and equity of redemption.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

**v. 3:** Gathering follows redemption. Spurgeon paints a picture of the Good Shepherd “who thus collects the blood-bought flock from the remotest regions.” He notes that the word translated “south” is really “the sea.” Guzik suggests the verse would be fitting in the mouth of Daniel, Ezra or Nehemiah, who had occasion to thank God for gathering a remnant from captivity. Ellicott says the phrase “the redeemed of the LORD” is taken from Isaiah 62:12 and “clearly denotes the Israelites who had been released from exile in Babylon and elsewhere.”
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/107.htm

---

### v. 4 — “Some wandered in desert wastelands, finding no path to a city in which to dwell.”

This opens the first vignette: the wanderers. Spurgeon describes them as “lost in the worst possible place, even as the sinner is who is lost in sin; they wandered up and down in vain searches and researches as a sinner does when he is awakened and sees his lost estate.” He notes the word “wandered” indicates not a purposeful journey but “an endless maze of desolation” (citing Hammond). The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary (PHC) notes the translation “in a solitary way” is better rendered “in a pathless waste” (Perowne) or “the pathless desert” (Hengstenberg): “the track is lost, perhaps obliterated by some violent sand-storm.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 5 — “They were hungry and thirsty; their soul fainted within them.”

Spurgeon observes: “The spirits sink when the bodily frame becomes exhausted by long privations. Who can keep his courage up when he is ready to fall to the ground at every step through utter exhaustion?” Spiritually, this pictures “an awakened conscience before it knows the Lord Jesus … full of unsatisfied cravings, painful needs, and heavy fears.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

---

### v. 6 — “Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress.”

This is the first occurrence of the refrain-pattern. Spurgeon notes: “Not till they were in extremities did they pray, but the mercy is that they prayed then, and prayed in the right manner, with a cry, and to the right person, even to the Lord.” He adds: “Some men will never pray till they are half starved, and for their best interests it is far better for them to be empty and faint than to be full and stouthearted. If hunger brings us to our knees it is more useful to us than feasting.” The PHC observes that this pattern shows prayer is “not only the resource of good men, but of all men in trouble. It is a natural instinct even of wicked men to turn to God at such times” (Perowne).
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 7 — “He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live.”

Spurgeon: “There are many wrong ways, but only one right one, and into this none can lead us but God himself. When the Lord is leader the way is sure to be right.” He contrasts human inability (“they found no city to dwell in”) with divine provision (“he found one readily enough”). The PHC calls the “city of habitation” a picture of the believer’s destination: “Here we have no continuing city, but we seek one to come.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 8 — “Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.”

The first refrain. Spurgeon says “men are not mentioned here in the original, but the word is fitly supplied” — the psalmist would have all creation magnify Jehovah. He laments: “They must be horrible ingrates who will not honour such a deliverer for so happy a rescue from the most cruel death.” Guzik notes we should thank God “for more than just His work in our personal lives, but also for what He does for others.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 9 — “For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.”

Spurgeon calls this “the summary of the lost traveller’s experience.” Spiritually: “The Lord sets us longing and then completely satisfies us. That longing leads us into solitude, separation, thirst, faintness and self-despair, and all these conduct us to prayer, faith, divine guidance, satisfying of the soul’s thirst, and rest.” Guzik notes that Mary the mother of Jesus quoted this verse in her Magnificat (Luke 1:53), showing “she was a woman who knew and loved God’s word.” VanGemeren (cited by Guzik) says: “His deliverance is full of surprises, as he supplies all the needs of his people.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 10 — “Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains.”

The second picture: prisoners. Spurgeon paints a grim scene: “The cell is dark of itself, and the fear of execution casts a still denser gloom over the prison. … tens of thousands have been made to linger in places only fit to be tombs.” He spiritualises: “The state of a soul under conviction of sin is forcibly symbolized by such a condition … they sit still in the inactivity of despair.” Matthew Poole notes “affliction and irons” may mean “afflicting or grievous irons” or “the cords of affliction” (cf. Job 36:8).
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 11 — “because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High.”

Spurgeon: “This was the general cause of bondage among the ancient people of God, they were given over to their adversaries because they were not loyal to the Lord. God’s words are not to be trifled with.” The PHC notes that this verse exhibits sin both in its guilt (rebellion against the supreme authority) and in its folly (rejection of the counsel of the wisest Being). Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) says: “He delivered them into the hands of their enemies, and, as they would not be under subjection to GOD, he delivered them into slavery to wicked men.… God had forsaken them because they had forsaken him.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 12 — “He humbled their hearts with hard labor; they stumbled, and there was no one to help.”

Spurgeon notes: “In eastern prisons men are frequently made to labour like beasts of the field. … This soon subdues the stoutest heart, and makes the proud boaster sing another tune. God has methods of abating the loftiness of rebellious looks; the cell and the mill make even giants tremble.” The PHC adds that the design of the captivity was to “subdue their pride” — “Their heart had proudly risen up in rebellion … and their captivity was designed by its sufferings to … show them their own helplessness, and that their strength and succour were in Him alone.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 13 — “Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.”

The second cry. Spurgeon remarks: “Not a prayer till then. While there was any to help below they would not look above. No cries till their hearts were brought down and their hopes were all dead — then they cried, but not before.” He adds: “They were long before they cried, but he was not long before he saved.” Trapp (cited by Guzik) says: “This is comfort to the greatest sinners; if they can but find a praying heart, God will find a pitying heart, and rebels shall be received with all sweetness.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 14 — “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains.”

Spurgeon presents an emphatically complete deliverance: “The Lord’s deliverances are of the most complete and triumphant kind, he neither leaves the soul in darkness nor in bonds, nor does he permit the powers of evil again to enthral the liberated captive. What he does is done for ever.” The PHC notes three features showing completeness: fetters riven asunder, prisoners brought out of the gloomy dungeon, and city gates broken down so they could go forth entirely.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 15 — “Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.”

The second refrain. Spurgeon: “The sight of such goodness makes a right-minded man long to see the Lord duly honoured for his amazing mercy. When dungeon doors fly open, and chains are snapped, who can refuse to adore the glorious goodness of the Lord? It makes the heart sick to think of such gracious mercies remaining unsung.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

---

### v. 16 — “For He has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.”

Spurgeon sees both a literal and spiritual sense. The PHC suggests “the gates of brass” refers probably to Babylon (cf. Isaiah 45:2). Spurgeon applies it spiritually: “The Lord Jesus has broken the most powerful of spiritual bonds and made us free indeed. Brass and iron are as tow before the flame of Jesus’ love. The gates of hell shall not prevail against us, neither shall the bars of the grave detain us.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 17 — “Fools, in their rebellious ways, and through their iniquities, suffered affliction.”

The third picture: the sick. Spurgeon states bluntly: “Many sicknesses are the direct result of foolish acts. Thoughtless and lustful men by drunkenness, gluttony, and the indulgence of their passions fill their bodies with diseases of the worst kind. Sin is at the bottom of all sorrow.” The PHC (following Perowne) translates it as: “Foolish men, because of the way of their transgression and because of their iniquities, bring affliction upon themselves.” It notes two principles: (1) wickedness is folly — the foolishness is moral, not intellectual; (2) wickedness leads to sickness — “The suffering was self-produced.” Kidner (cited by Guzik) says the verb points to trouble “as self-inflicted” and “verse 18 could well call to mind in modern times the drug-addict, but only as one example of man’s perennial determination to get hurt.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 18 — “They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death.”

Spurgeon: “Appetite departs from men when they are sick: the best of food is nauseous to them. … And they draw near unto the gates of death. From want of food, and from the destructive power of their malady, they slide gradually down till they lie at the door of the grave.” He applies it to souls under conviction of sin: “they cannot find comfort in the choicest promises, but turn away with loathing even from the gospel, so that they gradually decay into the grave of despair.” VanGemeren (cited by Guzik): “Their ‘affliction’ is a sickness to death, when food and pleasure are no longer relevant.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

---

### v. 19 — “Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.”

The third cry. Spurgeon says: “The fool lays aside his motley in prospect of the shroud, and betakes himself to his knees. What a cure for the soul sickness of body is often made to be by the Lord’s grace!” He adds: “When we have no appetite for meat we may have an appetite for prayer. He who cannot feed on the word of God may yet turn to God himself and find mercy.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

---

### v. 20 — “He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit.”

Spurgeon declares: “Man is not healed by medicine alone, but by the word which proceedeth out of the mouth of God is man restored from going down to the grave. A word will do it, a word has done it thousands of times.” He then moves to the spiritual: “Sin-sick souls should remember the power of the Word. … Christ, the eternal Word, comes with healing power in the direst extremity, saving to the uttermost.” He also relates a historical account of the Reformer George Wishart preaching on this very verse at Dundee during the plague of 1545, to great effect.

Ellicott compares this to Psalm 105:19 and 147:18 — God’s word is His messenger — and to Isaiah 55:10–11. The PHC (citing Perowne) detects here “the first glimmering of St. John’s doctrine of the agency of the personal Word.” Constable notes: “The reference to God’s Word having a part in their healing shows that spiritual nourishment plays a vital part in physical restoration (cf. Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4; James 5:14–16).”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/107.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-107.html

---

### v. 21 — “Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.”

The third refrain. Spurgeon notes wryly: “It is marvellous that men can be restored from sickness and yet refuse to bless the Lord. … Yet when ten are healed it is seldom that more than one returns to give glory to God. Alas, where are the nine?” He concludes: “When a spiritual cure is wrought by the great Physician, praise is one of the surest signs of renewed health.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

---

### v. 22 — “Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing.”

Spurgeon: “In such a case let there be gifts and oblations as well as words. Let the good Physician have his fee of gratitude. Let life become a sacrifice to him who has prolonged it.” He adds that declaring God’s works “honours God, relieves ourselves, comforts others, and puts all men in possession of facts concerning the divine goodness.” The PHC notes this final call moves beyond mere words to “sacrifices of thanksgiving” — public, costly acts of gratitude.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-107.html

---

## Points of Differing Emphasis Across Protestant Traditions

From the sources accessed, several distinct emphases emerge:

**Baptist (Spurgeon, spurgeon.org):** A strong emphasis on the spiritual/allegorical reading, where the four physical deliverances are “types and shadows” of spiritual salvation — the wanderer is the lost sinner, the prisoner is the soul under conviction, the sick man is the sin-sick soul, etc. Spurgeon also maintains a Calvinistic emphasis on divine sovereignty in deliverance (“His own unaided arm has wrought out their deliverance”) while also stressing human responsibility to cry out. His language about v. 20 — “Christ, the eternal Word, comes with healing power” — is strongly Christocentric.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps107.php

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik, while largely following the traditional reading, makes a point of the direct connection between Psalm 107 and the healing ministry of Jesus (“reminding us of the many times Jesus healed people simply by speaking a word”). He also highlights the application of v. 20 to the believer today, that “what we want most of all is to have that word sent home by the power of the Holy Spirit” (quoting Spurgeon). His emphasis on the Spirit’s present, experiential work is characteristic of charismatic reading.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-107/

**Evangelical (Constable, studylight.org):** Constable takes a more historical-grammatical approach, linking the psalm to the post-exilic period and viewing the four deliverances as answers to Solomon’s temple dedication prayer. He ties v. 20 to Deuteronomy 8:3, Matthew 4:4 and James 5:14–16, emphasising that “spiritual nourishment plays a vital part in physical restoration.” His focus is on the psalm as a wisdom psalm that teaches God’s people to “observe God’s loyalty to them.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-107.html

## What Could Not Be Found (Due to Search/Fetch Limits)

- **Reformed views (Ligonier, monergism.com):** No dedicated Reformed commentary pages were returned in the searches.
- **Lutheran views (lcms.org, 1517.org):** No results were found.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan views (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com):** No results were found.
- **Anglican views:** Ryle’s or other Anglican commentaries on Psalm 107 were not retrieved.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org):** No search results were returned.
- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org):** Not reached.
- **Prosperity/Word of Faith teaching on v. 20:** The dedicated search returned no results. However, it is well known anecdotally that Psalm 107:20 (“He sent His word and healed them”) is frequently cited in Word of Faith circles as a proof-text for physical healing through confessing Scripture. None of the sites within the permitted list were found to discuss or critique this usage.
